items.title: Affine spaces over a real vector space and displacement vectors
items.statement: Let V be a real vector space. An affine space over V is a nonempty set A together with a map +: A x V -> A such that (a) (p+v)+w = p+(v+w) and p+0 = p for all p in A and v,w in V, and (b) for all p,q in A there is exactly one v in V with p+v = q. That unique v is written q-p and called the displacement from p to q. Then p+(q-p) = q, p-p = 0, p+0 = p, (q-p)+(r-q) = r-p, and for each p in A the map v |-> p+v is a bijection A -> A. If V is 4-dimensional and E: R^4 -> V is a linear isomorphism, then x(p) := E^{-1}(p-o) is a bijection A -> R^4 for each o in A; such maps are the affine coordinate systems on A.
items.strategy: The uniqueness clause (b) is what makes q-p well defined. The identities follow from the action axioms and uniqueness: p+(q-p) = q is the defining property of q-p; p-p = 0 and p+0 = p come from p+0 = p; and p+[(q-p)+(r-q)] = [p+(q-p)]+(r-q) = q+(r-q) = r = p+(r-p) gives (q-p)+(r-q) = r-p by uniqueness. For each p, v |-> p+v is surjective by (b) and injective because an equality p+v = p+w and the action axioms give p+(v-w) = p = p+0, so v-w = 0 by (b) applied at (p,p).

items.title: Lorentz forms of inertia (3,1,0) on a 4-dimensional real vector space
items.statement: Let V be a 4-dimensional real vector space. A Lorentz form on V is a symmetric bilinear form eta: V x V -> R that is nondegenerate (both radicals are {0}) and has inertia (3,1,0): in some (equivalently, by Sylvester's law of inertia, in every) basis diagonalizing eta there are exactly three positive diagonal entries, exactly one negative diagonal entry, and no zero diagonal entry. The associated quadratic form is q(v) := eta(v,v). The pair (V,eta) is called a Lorentz vector space of signature (-,+,+,+).
items.strategy: Nondegeneracy is the statement that the radicals vanish; for finite-dimensional V it is equivalent to invertibility of the matrix of eta in any basis and hence to the absence of zero diagonal entries in every diagonalizing basis (the radical is the kernel of the associated map V -> V*, so its dimension is dim V minus the rank). The inertia (3,1,0) is the Sylvester normal form diag(I_3,-I_1,0_0) of the definition of definiteness/inertia; Sylvester's law makes it basis-independent. No positive-definite structure on V is assumed.

items.title: Timelike, null, spacelike and causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space. A vector v in V is timelike if eta(v,v) < 0, null (or lightlike) if v is nonzero and eta(v,v) = 0, spacelike if eta(v,v) > 0, and causal if it is timelike or null. The zero vector is none of timelike, null or spacelike. The sign of eta(v,v) is the causal character of v. The pairing eta itself is written <v,w> := eta(v,w) when no confusion arises. Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.
items.strategy: The classification is by the sign of the real number eta(v,v); the three alternatives eta(v,v) < 0, eta(v,v) = 0, eta(v,v) > 0 for v nonzero are mutually exclusive and exhaustive by trichotomy of the order on R, and the zero vector is excluded from the null case by definition.

items.title: Every Lorentz form admits an ordered basis with matrix diag(-1,1,1,1)
items.statement: Let eta be a Lorentz form on a 4-dimensional real vector space V. There is an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V with eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab} for all a,b. Such a basis is called eta-orthonormal; in every eta-orthonormal ordered basis exactly one basis vector is timelike and the other three are spacelike, and the count is the inertia (3,1,0) of eta.
items.strategy: Sylvester's law of inertia supplies a basis in which the matrix of eta is the normal form diag(I_p,-I_q,0_r) with (p,q,r) the inertia of eta. The definition of a Lorentz form gives (p,q,r) = (3,1,0), so the matrix is diag(1,1,1,-1); reindexing the basis puts the single negative entry in the first slot and yields diag(-1,1,1,1). Since inertia is independent of the diagonalizing basis, every eta-orthonormal basis exhibits the same count.

items.title: eta-orthogonality and orthogonal complements in a Lorentz vector space
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space. Vectors u,v are eta-orthogonal, written u orthogonal v, if eta(u,v) = 0. For a subset S of V the orthogonal complement is S^perp := {v in V : eta(v,s) = 0 for all s in S}, and for a vector u one writes u^perp := {u}^perp. For all subsets S the set S^perp is a linear subspace of V, S is contained in (S^perp)^perp, and S^perp = (span S)^perp; in particular u belongs to u^perp exactly when eta(u,u) = 0. Unlike a positive-definite inner product, a nonzero vector can be orthogonal to itself.
items.strategy: Bilinearity gives that S^perp is closed under addition and scalar multiplication (each condition eta(.,s) = 0 is linear), and the containments and the equality S^perp = (span S)^perp follow by linearity in the second argument. The final sentence is witnessed by the classification: any nonzero null vector v satisfies eta(v,v) = 0, so v lies in v^perp.

items.title: Time orientation, future and past timelike/null/causal vectors, and the closed cones
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space and let T := {v in V : eta(v,v) < 0} be its timelike set. By the components lemma T has exactly two connected components; a time orientation of (V,eta) is a choice of one of them. Fixing such a choice and writing C^+ for the chosen component and C^- := T \ C^+ for the other, call v future timelike if v is in C^+, past timelike if v is in C^-, future null if v is nonzero, eta(v,v) = 0 and v lies in the closure cl(C^+), past null if v is nonzero, eta(v,v) = 0 and v lies in cl(C^-), future causal if it is future timelike or future null, and past causal if it is past timelike or past null. The sets cl(C^+) and cl(C^-) are the future and past closed cones; they are convex cones meeting only at 0, and a causal vector is future or past but not both.
items.strategy: Well-definedness rests on the components lemma: T has exactly two components, so 'a choice of one of them' names a definite pair {C^+,C^-}. The claimed properties of the closures (convexity, the intersection {0}, and exclusivity of the future and past causal sets) are proved in the components lemma via the orthonormal coordinate description {v^0 >= |v_vec|} and {v^0 <= -|v_vec|} of the two closed cones.

items.title: The timelike set has exactly two convex components, described in orthonormal coordinates
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a Lorentz vector space and let (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an eta-orthonormal ordered basis; write v = v^0 e_0 + v^1 e_1 + v^2 e_2 + v^3 e_3 and |v_vec| := sqrt((v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2). Then eta(v,v) = -(v^0)^2 + |v_vec|^2, and the timelike set T = {v : eta(v,v) < 0} satisfies T = T_+ union T_- with T_+ := {v : v^0 > |v_vec|} and T_- := {v : v^0 < -|v_vec|}. The sets T_+ and T_- are nonempty, disjoint, open in V, convex and path-connected, and they are exactly the two connected components of T; in every eta-orthonormal basis whose first vector is timelike the same description holds, with the two displayed sets possibly interchanged. Moreover cl(T_+) = {v : v^0 >= |v_vec|}, cl(T_-) = {v : v^0 <= -|v_vec|}, and cl(T_+) intersection cl(T_-) = {0}.
items.strategy: In the orthonormal basis, eta(v,v) = -(v^0)^2 + sum_i (v^i)^2, so eta(v,v) < 0 iff |v^0| > |v_vec|, which is the displayed union; the two sets are disjoint and nonempty (e_0 lies in the first, -e_0 in the second). Convexity of T_+: for u,w in T_+ and t in [0,1], (tu+(1-t)w)^0 = t u^0 + (1-t) w^0 > t|u_vec| + (1-t)|w_vec| >= |t u_vec + (1-t) w_vec| by the triangle inequality; T_- is handled by applying this to -v. Convex sets are path-connected, and T_+ and T_- are open (they are the preimages of (0,inf) under the continuous maps v |-> v^0 - |v_vec| and v |-> -v^0 - |v_vec|). Since T is the disjoint union of two nonempty relatively open connected sets, it is disconnected and these are its two components: any connected subset of T lies in one of them, because a connected subset meeting both would give a separation, while a path in T cannot change the sign of the continuous function v^0 (which is nowhere zero on T) by the intermediate value theorem. The closures are computed by continuity of v^0 -/+ |v_vec|; their intersection consists of vectors with v^0 >= |v_vec| and v^0 <= -|v_vec|, hence of 0 alone. Finally, any two orthonormal bases are related by a linear isomorphism, and the components of T are intrinsic to eta, so the coordinate description agrees with the components up to the naming of T_+ and T_-.

items.title: Oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (the spacetime primitives)
items.statement: An oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space is a quadruple (A,V,eta,C^+) consisting of: a nonempty affine space A over a 4-dimensional real vector space V (def-affine-space-and-displacement); a Lorentz form eta on V (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia); an orientation of V, i.e. a positive ray of the determinant line Lambda^4 V, fixed once and for all (def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space); and a time orientation C^+ of (V,eta) (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). The points of A are called events; q-p is the displacement from p to q; the interval of p,q in A is I(p,q) := eta(q-p,q-p); and p,q are timelike, null, spacelike or causally related when q-p is timelike, null, spacelike or causal, future-related when q-p is future causal, and past-related when q-p is past causal (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). No point of A is distinguished: for every v in V the translation p |-> p+v is a bijection of A preserving all the structure except the labelling of points. All later structure of this framework (frames, charts, tensor fields, worldlines) is built on this model, and no derived physical quantity is part of it.
items.strategy: The definition is a structure specification: the affine action, the form, the orientation and the time orientation are separately defined objects, and the definition only bundles them and fixes the terminology (events, displacement, interval, causal relations). Well-definedness of the bundled data requires the existence and uniqueness statements supplied by the cited items: affine coordinates are available by the affine-space definition, the orthonormal basis needed later exists by the orthonormal-basis lemma, and the two components of the timelike set needed to choose C^+ exist by the components lemma. The translation invariance claim follows from the affine axioms: displacements are unchanged by translations, and translations have identity linear part, so they preserve eta, the orientation and C^+.

items.title: Inertial frames and inertial charts of the affine Minkowski model
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space. An inertial frame of the model is a tuple (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) consisting of an event o in A and an ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) of V that is eta-orthonormal (eta(e_a,e_b) = diag(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}), future (e_0 is in C^+) and positively oriented (the ordered basis class of (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is the fixed orientation of V). Its inertial chart is the map x: A -> R^4, x(p) := E^{-1}(p-o), where E: R^4 -> V is the linear isomorphism E(u) := sum_a u^a e_a; its components x^a(p) are the inertial coordinates of the event p, and x(p) = 0 exactly at p = o. The family of all inertial frames and charts is the inertial atlas of the model; two inertial charts x, x' are related by x' = M^{-1}(x - x(o')) for M the change-of-basis matrix between the two ordered bases, so transitions are affine bijections of R^4.
items.strategy: Well-definedness requires the existence of eta-orthonormal bases (orthonormal-basis lemma) and the possibility of making them future and positively oriented (existence lemma below). The transition formula follows from the definitions: if e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b, then for p = o + sum_a x^a e_a one has p = o' + sum_a x'^a e'_a with x' = M^{-1}(x - x(o')), because applying E'^{-1} to the displacement identity p - o' = (p-o) + (o-o') gives exactly that expression; that x' = 0 iff p = o' is then immediate.

items.title: Existence of future-oriented inertial frames at every event
items.statement: In every oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (A,V,eta,C^+) and for every event o in A there exists an inertial frame with origin o; consequently inertial charts are defined at every event. Explicitly: start from any eta-orthonormal ordered basis (f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3) of V; if f_0 is not in C^+ then replacing f_0 by -f_0 makes the first vector future (because the timelike set is the disjoint union of C^+ and C^- and eta(-f_0,-f_0) = eta(f_0,f_0)); the resulting ordered basis has some orientation class, and if that class is negative (det M = -1 relative to the fixed orientation) then replacing e_1 by -e_1 (or interchanging e_1 and e_2) produces a positively oriented ordered basis, without destroying eta-orthonormality and without changing the first, future vector.
items.strategy: Apply the orthonormal-basis lemma to get f_0,...,f_3. Since eta(f_0,f_0) = -1 < 0, f_0 lies in the timelike set T = C^+ disjoint-union C^-, so exactly one of f_0, -f_0 lies in C^+. Negating a basis vector preserves eta-orthonormality because eta is bilinear and (-1)^2 = 1, and negating one vector changes the orientation class by the sign of the change-of-basis matrix, which is -1; hence at most one further negation (or the interchange of two vectors, also of determinant -1) makes the ordered basis positively oriented while preserving eta-orthonormality and the future first vector. The origin o is appended freely since frames are allowed any origin.

items.title: The affine atlas makes the Minkowski model a smooth 4-manifold diffeomorphic to R^4
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let x: A -> R^4 be one inertial chart. Give A the topology in which a set U is open exactly when x(U) is open in R^4 (the transported topology; it is the unique topology making x a homeomorphism onto R^4). Then: (i) A is a Hausdorff, second-countable topological 4-manifold; (ii) the one-chart family {x} is a smooth atlas, so A is a smooth 4-manifold and x is a diffeomorphism onto R^4 with its standard smooth structure; (iii) every affine chart of A, i.e. every map of the form y(p) = M x(p) + b with M an invertible 4x4 real matrix and b in R^4, and in particular every inertial chart, belongs to the same smooth structure, and its transition with x is the smooth diffeomorphism u |-> M u + b of R^4 with inverse u |-> M^{-1}(u-b); (iv) the topology and smooth structure do not depend on the choice of the initial inertial chart x.
items.strategy: For (i): x is by construction a homeomorphism A -> R^4; R^4 is Hausdorff, second-countable and locally Euclidean, and each of these properties transfers along a homeomorphism (separate points by preimages of disjoint open neighbourhoods; pull back a countable basis; use x itself as a global coordinate chart). For (ii): a one-chart family vacuously satisfies smooth compatibility, so {x} is a smooth atlas; the maximal atlas it generates is the smooth structure, and in this structure the coordinate representation of x is the identity, so x is a diffeomorphism onto R^4 equipped with the standard structure. For (iii): if y = M x + b is an affine chart, then y is a homeomorphism for the same topology and the transition y o x^{-1} is the map u |-> M u + b, whose components are polynomials of degree at most 1 in the coordinates; linear maps and constant maps of R^4 are smooth, and sums of smooth functions are smooth, so y o x^{-1} is smooth (one can differentiate componentwise using the algebra of total derivatives and the theorem that continuous partial derivatives imply total differentiability). Its inverse u |-> M^{-1}(u-b) is again affine and smooth, so y belongs to the same smooth structure; every inertial chart has this form by the transition formula of the frame definition. For (iv): if x' is another inertial chart, then x' = M x + b for an affine map of the displayed form, so the topologies transported by x and x' coincide and the two suggested one-chart atlases generate the same maximal atlas.

items.title: The tangent space of the affine Minkowski model at any event is canonically V
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with its smooth structure and let p be an event. For a smooth germ [f] at p define Phi_p(v)([f]) := (d/dt)|_{t=0} f(p+tv). Then Phi_p: V -> T_pA is a linear isomorphism of V onto the tangent space T_pA; in particular T_pA is canonically identified with V, independently of any chart. If x is an inertial chart and v = v^0 e_0 + v^1 e_1 + v^2 e_2 + v^3 e_3, then the coordinate derivations at p correspond under this identification to partial_a = e_a, i.e. Phi_p(v) = sum_a v^a partial_a|_p.
items.strategy: Well-definedness: for a smooth germ [f] the curve c(t) := p + t v has, in the inertial chart x, the coordinate representation x(p) + t u with u = E^{-1} v, hence is smooth; therefore f o c is smooth near 0 and the derivative at 0 exists. Differentiation of products of smooth functions gives Phi_p(v)([fg]) = f(p) Phi_p(v)([g]) + g(p) Phi_p(v)([f]) by the product rule, so each Phi_p(v) is a derivation, and Phi_p is linear in v by the chain rule applied to t |-> x(p) + t u. Injectivity: if Phi_p(v) = 0 and x is an inertial chart at p with coordinates x^a, then applying Phi_p(v) to the germs x^a - x^a(p) gives v^a for each a, so v = 0. Bijectivity: the coordinate derivations partial_0,...,partial_3 form a basis of T_pA, so dim T_pA = 4 = dim V, and an injective linear map between these spaces is an isomorphism. Canonicity: the curve t |-> p + tv is defined by the affine structure alone, so Phi_p does not depend on the chart; the final display follows from the coordinate computation in the chart.

items.title: The oriented volume form epsilon and the permutation symbols of an inertial frame
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let (o;e_0,...,e_3) be an inertial frame. For v_0,...,v_3 in V let [v_j^a] be the 4x4 matrix whose j-th column lists the coordinates of v_j in the ordered basis (e_0,...,e_3), and define epsilon(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3) := det([v_j^a]) in the sense of the determinant of a square matrix. Then epsilon is an alternating 4-linear form on V, called the oriented volume form of the model. Its components in the inertial frame are the permutation symbols epsilon_{abcd}, with epsilon_{0123} = +1 and epsilon_{abcd} the sign of the permutation taking (0,1,2,3) to (a,b,c,d) (zero if two indices repeat). The raised components are epsilon^{abcd} := eta^{aa'} eta^{bb'} eta^{cc'} eta^{dd'} epsilon_{a'b'c'd'}, where eta^{ab} is the inverse of the matrix eta_{ab}; epsilon^{0123} = -1. The spatial permutation symbol epsilon_{ijk} for i,j,k in {1,2,3} is defined by epsilon_{123} = +1 together with alternation.
items.strategy: epsilon is the determinant of the coordinate matrix of (v_0,...,v_3); the determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns, hence epsilon is an alternating 4-linear form. Its components in the frame are by definition the determinant values, i.e. the permutation-sign symbols; epsilon^{0123} computes to eta^{00}eta^{11}eta^{22}eta^{33} epsilon_{0123} = (-1)(+1)(+1)(+1)(+1) = -1 because the inverse metric is diagonal in an eta-orthonormal frame. Well-definedness of epsilon as a form of the model, independent of the inertial frame used, is proved in the frame-independence lemma.

items.title: The oriented volume form is independent of the positively oriented inertial frame
items.statement: The alternating 4-linear form epsilon of def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form does not depend on the inertial frame used to define it: if (e'_0,...,e'_3) is another inertial frame and e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b is the change-of-basis matrix, then det M = +1 (both ordered bases are positively oriented) and the coordinate matrices X, X' of a tuple (v_0,...,v_3) in the two frames satisfy X' = M^{-1} X, so det X' = det(M^{-1}) det X = det X. Consequently epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) = 1 for every inertial frame, epsilon is the unique alternating 4-linear form on V taking value 1 on every positively oriented eta-orthonormal basis, and in every inertial frame the raised component epsilon^{0123} equals -1.
items.strategy: From eta(e'_a,e'_b) = eta_{ab} and e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b one gets the matrix identity M^T eta M = eta; taking determinants and using det eta = -1 gives (det M)^2 = 1, so det M = +1 or -1, and the orientation clause selects det M = +1. The coordinate columns of a fixed tuple in the two bases are related by X' = M^{-1} X, so multiplicativity of the determinant and det(M^{-1}) = (det M)^{-1} give det X' = det X; this is exactly the frame independence, and it also shows the normalized value 1 on the frame itself. Uniqueness of the normalized alternating 4-linear form is the uniqueness clause for the determinant as a normalized alternating multilinear function, transported to V by the coordinate isomorphism E. The raised component computation is the diagonal evaluation given in the definition.

items.title: SI units and coordinate conventions of the special-relativity framework
items.statement: This framework fixes the following SI coordinate and unit conventions. In every inertial chart the coordinates are x^0 = c t, x^1, x^2, x^3, where c > 0 is the adopted conversion constant in metres per second and the spatial coordinates are measured in metres along the frame's orthonormal spatial directions; all four x^a carry the unit metre, the matrix of eta in an inertial chart is diag(-1,1,1,1) with dimensionless entries, and the interval I(p,q) carries the unit m^2. For a timelike displacement the number tau := c^{-1} sqrt(-eta(q-p,q-p)) has the unit second and is the proper time of the straight timelike segment from p to q. A timelike worldline's four-velocity U = dx/dtau has unit m/s, four-acceleration m/s^2, four-momentum kg m/s, and observer energy joule. If instead a chart uses a temporal coordinate t in seconds, then the corresponding metric component is g_tt = -c^2 with unit m^2/s^2 and the mixed time-space components acquire the unit m/s; formulas derived in one convention are not reused unchanged in the other. Natural units (c = 1) may be used only together with an explicit restoration table for c. The numerical value of c is an empirical parameter of the model; SI unit status does not make a quantity primitive in this theory.
items.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalization (x^0 = ct rather than t), the unit of each component, and the dimensional interpretation of the interval, of proper time along a timelike straight segment and of the derived kinematic quantities, all relative to the adopted model and its inertial charts. The dimensional statements follow by inspection of the inertial coordinate expressions out of the diagonal form of eta, and the warning about the temporal-coordinate convention records where the components change dimension.

items.title: Adopted inertial covariance of the model equations
items.statement: Adopt as a physical assumption of this framework: (i) the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (A,V,eta,C^+) is the spacetime of the framework; its points represent idealized physical events, displacements represent idealized spacetime separations, and the sign classification of eta is the adopted causal structure; (ii) the equations of the specific mechanical and electromagnetic models developed from this framework are covariant under the affine maps F: A -> A whose linear part L satisfies eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V, has determinant +1 relative to the adopted orientation, and maps C^+ onto C^+; such maps are the inertial changes of description. These assumptions are adopted, not deduced from experiment nor from the verbal postulates of Einstein, and they define the framework's scope. Covariance is asserted for the specified model equations only: it does not select a force or matter law, does not forbid explicitly adopted background structure by a purely syntactic test, and carries no claim that the physical world is exactly described by the model.
items.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: the item records the adopted formulation (affine Minkowski geometry with a fixed orientation and future cone) and the adopted covariance of the framework's model equations under future- and orientation-preserving eta-isometries of V. The maps are characterized by their defining properties rather than by a named group; the group structure, factorization and algebra of these maps are established on the Lorentz-transformations page. The exposition must state the scope limitation that covariance is a property of the specified model equations and neither proves the model nor selects dynamics.

Excludes gravity (no curvature), global accelerated-frame structure, and quantum effects. Covariance is claimed only for the mechanical and electromagnetic model equations specified in this framework.

items.title: Adopted ideal-clock and ideal-vacuum-light interpretation
items.statement: Adopt as physical assumptions of this framework: (i) Ideal clocks. Along a curve x: I -> A whose coordinate representation in an inertial chart is C^1 with everywhere future timelike derivative, an ideal clock carried along the curve reads, between parameters a < b in I, the elapsed time sigma(b) - sigma(a) = c^{-1} integral_a^b sqrt(-eta(x'(s),x'(s))) ds; there is no additional acceleration-dependent term in the reading (clock hypothesis). (ii) Ideal light. In vacuum, ideal light rays are exactly the future null straight lines {p + lambda v : lambda in R} with p in A and v a future null vector; in every inertial chart x^a such a ray has x(lambda) = x(p) + lambda (v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3) and coordinate speed c, so the adopted conversion constant c is the same in all inertial charts. Scope: ideal apparatus, complete vacuum, and the geometric (nondispersive) ray regime. The assumptions are adopted, not experimentally proved; no dispersive medium is described; no quantum photon model is assumed and in particular frequency is not identified with energy by a factor hbar; and real clocks and light are not claimed to be exactly ideal.
items.strategy: A postulate, not a theorem: it fixes the physical interpretation of the mathematical objects (future timelike curves, future null straight lines) and the reading rule of an ideal clock, together with the exact scope of the idealization. The integral is well defined because the integrand -eta(x',x') is positive and continuous on a compact parameter interval for a future timelike C^1 curve; parametrization invariance and the resulting proper-time parametrization, as well as the general theory of worldlines, four-velocity and acceleration, are developed on the later worldlines-and-clocks page, which may not depend on this page by a forward edge; the postulate therefore states the reading rule for the model rather than a theorem about curves.

items.title: The Euclidean spatial structure and cross product of an inertial frame
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame. Put S := span(e_1,e_2,e_3) = {w in V : eta(e_0,w) = 0} and let delta be the restriction of eta to S. Then delta is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form on S (the Euclidean spatial form of the frame), |w| := sqrt(delta(w,w)) is a norm on S, and (e_1,e_2,e_3) is a delta-orthonormal positively oriented ordered basis of S. Writing w = w^1 e_1 + w^2 e_2 + w^3 e_3, define the vector product w x z as the unique element of S with components ((w x z)^1,(w x z)^2,(w x z)^3) = (w^2 z^3 - w^3 z^2, w^3 z^1 - w^1 z^3, w^1 z^2 - w^2 z^1). Then delta(w x z, y) equals the determinant of the coordinate matrix with columns w,z,y for every y in S, and |w x z|^2 = |w|^2 |z|^2 - delta(w,z)^2. All these objects belong to the positive spatial three-space of the named inertial frame: they are equivariant under orientation-preserving spatial rotations of the frame and are not invariant under a general Lorentz map. The invariant structure of the model remains eta alone.
items.strategy: Since (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is eta-orthonormal, for w = sum_i w^i e_i one has eta(e_0,w) = 0 and eta(w,w) = sum_i (w^i)^2, so the restriction delta is positive definite and (e_1,e_2,e_3) is delta-orthonormal; positivity of eta(w,w) on S also shows S = e_0^perp. The vector product is well defined by its displayed coordinate formula, and the identity delta(w x z,y) = det(w,z,y) is Lagrange's identity for the cross product in an orthonormal basis; the norm identity is the same computation in coordinates. Frame dependence: a general eta-orthonormal frame has a different time axis e_0 and hence a different S, so the construction depends on the frame; the final sentence records that only eta is invariant.

items.title: Primitive and derived notions of the spacetime-primitives page
items.statement: Status audit of the framework's adopted and derived notions, required before derived claims. Primitive mathematical structure of the model (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model): the affine space A with its action of V, the Lorentz form eta, the orientation of V and the time-orientation component C^+. Primitive physical interpretation and parameters adopted on this page: the physical event interpretation and the covariance assumption (post-sr-inertial-covariance); the ideal-clock and ideal-vacuum-light interpretation (post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light); and the conversion constant c, whose numerical value is empirical and whose unit is fixed by def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions. Derived (constructed, not adopted) on this page: displacements and intervals; the causal classification of displacements; inertial frames and their charts; the smooth structure; the oriented volume form; and the spatial Euclidean structure of a named inertial frame. Not introduced on this page and not primitive in its scope: proper time along general worldlines, four-velocity and four-acceleration, momentum, energy, charge and any force or matter law; later pages introduce their own adopted premises and must repeat this audit for them. The mathematical statements of this page concern the stipulated geometry only and do not assert that the model describes nature.
items.strategy: A status remark: it repeats, without proof obligations, the primitive/derived classification of the page's objects as required by the framework content model, and separates the mathematically constructed structure from the physically adopted interpretation. It carries no claim beyond that bookkeeping.

items.title: Worked affine transition between two inertial charts
items.statement: Worked computation of the transition between two inertial charts. Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space with inertial frames (o;e_a) and (o';e'_a) and charts x, x', and write e'_a = sum_b M^b_a e_b with M invertible. Then for every event p, x'(p) = M^{-1}(x(p) - x(o')) = M^{-1} x(p) + b with b := -M^{-1} x(o'), so the transition is affine. Explicit 1+1-dimensional case: V = R^2 with eta(v,w) = -v^0 w^0 + v^1 w^1, o = o' = 0, e_0 = (1,0), e_1 = (0,1), and the boosted inertial frame e'_0 = (cosh r, sinh r), e'_1 = (sinh r, cosh r) for real r, which satisfies eta(e'_0,e'_0) = -1, eta(e'_1,e'_1) = +1, eta(e'_0,e'_1) = 0 and det M = cosh^2 r - sinh^2 r = 1 with M the matrix with columns e'_0, e'_1 in the e-basis. The transition matrix is M^{-1} = [[cosh r, -sinh r],[-sinh r, cosh r]], and x'(o) = 0, x'(x^{-1}(1,0)) = (cosh r, -sinh r).
items.strategy: Substitute the definitions: E'(u) = u^0 e'_0 + u^1 e'_1 = E(M u), so E'^{-1} = M^{-1} E^{-1} and x'(p) = M^{-1}(x(p) - x(o')). The 1+1 verification is by direct multiplication using cosh^2 r - sinh^2 r = 1: the metric identities for e'_0, e'_1 and the determinant-one orientation identity are finite computations, and the two displayed transition values follow from the matrix inverse written explicitly.

items.title: Worked causal classification of explicit displacements
items.statement: Worked classification in an inertial frame of the model. With eta = diag(-1,1,1,1) in the frame, compute: v = (1,1,0,0) has eta(v,v) = 0 and v^0 = 1 = |v_vec|, so v is future null; w = (2,1,0,0) has eta(w,w) = -4+1 = -3 < 0 and w^0 = 2 > 1 = |w_vec|, so w is future timelike; z = (1,2,0,0) has eta(z,z) = -1+4 = 3 > 0, so z is spacelike; u = (-1,1,0,0) has eta(u,u) = 0 and u^0 = -1 < 0, so u is past null; e_0 = (1,0,0,0) is future timelike with eta = -1 and -e_0 is past timelike. In particular no future causal displacement is spacelike and the coordinated descriptions v^0 >= |v_vec| (future causal) and v^0 <= -|v_vec| (past causal) reproduce the sign classification.
items.strategy: All values are direct evaluations of the displayed diagonal form; membership in the future or past cone is decided by the sign of v^0 and the coordinate description of the closed cones proved in the components lemma. Each line is a finite arithmetic check, so the example is a complete computation from the definitions rather than a new result.

items.title: Worked orthogonal complement of a timelike displacement is positive definite
items.statement: Worked computation. In an inertial frame with eta = diag(-1,1,1,1) take u = (2,1,0,0), a future timelike displacement with eta(u,u) = -3. A displacement v = (v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3) is eta-orthogonal to u exactly when -2 v^0 + v^1 = 0, i.e. v^1 = 2 v^0. On that hyperplane eta(v,v) = -(v^0)^2 + (2v^0)^2 + (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2 = 3(v^0)^2 + (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2, which is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at v = 0. Hence the restriction of eta to u^perp is positive definite and every nonzero displacement orthogonal to a timelike displacement is spacelike.
items.strategy: Evaluate eta(u,.) = 0 and expand the quadratic form in the coordinates; positivity and the vanishing locus are read off the sum 3(v^0)^2 + (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2, completing the worked computation from the definitions.

items.title: The orthogonal complement of a null vector need not be positive definite
items.statement: Statement refuted: 'for every nonzero displacement u of a Lorentz vector space the restriction of eta to u^perp is positive definite'. Counterexample: in an inertial frame with eta = diag(-1,1,1,1) take u = (1,1,0,0). Then eta(u,u) = 0, so u is null and nonzero; the conditions eta(u,v) = 0 read -v^0 + v^1 = 0, so v^1 = v^0 and eta(v,v) = (v^2)^2 + (v^3)^2. This is nonnegative on u^perp and vanishes exactly on the one-dimensional subspace span(u), so the restriction of eta to u^perp is positive semidefinite but not positive definite; in particular u itself is orthogonal to u. The timelike case is genuinely different, as the companion example shows.
items.strategy: Direct computation with the displayed diagonal form: eta(u,u) = -1 + 1 = 0; expanding eta(u,v) = 0 solves the orthogonality condition; expanding eta(v,v) shows the restriction is positive semidefinite with kernel span(u), which refutes positive definiteness.

items.title: The causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space are not closed under addition
items.statement: Statement refuted: 'the set of causal vectors of a Lorentz vector space is a linear subspace, in particular closed under addition'. Counterexample: in an inertial frame with eta = diag(-1,1,1,1), let u = (1,0,0,0) and w = (-1,9/10,0,0). Then eta(u,u) = -1 < 0 and eta(w,w) = -1 + 81/100 = -19/100 < 0, so both u and w are timelike (u future, w past); but u + w = (0,9/10,0,0) has eta(u+w,u+w) = 81/100 > 0 and is spacelike. Moreover -u is causal but not future causal, so the future causal set is not closed under negation either. Closure of the full causal set under addition therefore fails; the future causal cone is closed under addition of future causal vectors, and that distinct statement belongs to the causality page.
items.strategy: Evaluate the diagonal form on the displayed vectors: the two timelike verifications and the spacelike value of the sum are finite arithmetic. The sentence about the future cone records that no claim is made here about sums of future causal vectors; that closure is proved later.

items.title: Worked component signs of the oriented volume form
items.statement: Worked computation of the volume-form components in an inertial frame with epsilon(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) = +1. The covariant components are the permutation signs: epsilon_{0123} = +1, epsilon_{0213} = -1 (one transposition), epsilon_{2301} = +1 (the product of the two transpositions (0 2) and (1 3)), epsilon_{3210} = +1 (the product of the two transpositions (0 3) and (1 2)), and epsilon_{a b c d} = 0 whenever two indices coincide. Raising all indices with the diagonal inverse metric gives epsilon^{0123} = eta^{00} eta^{11} eta^{22} eta^{33} epsilon_{0123} = -1. For the spatial symbol, epsilon_{123} = +1, epsilon_{213} = -1, epsilon_{312} = +1, and epsilon_{ijk} = 0 if two spatial indices coincide.
items.strategy: Each value is a determinant or permutation-sign computation in the displayed frame, using the definition of the volume form; the raised component is the single nonzero diagonal term of the sum, as computed in the definition; the spatial symbol is the three-dimensional restriction of the same product with the frame's positive spatial orientation.

items.title: The Lorentz form is not an inner product
items.statement: Statement refuted: 'the Lorentz form eta of a Lorentz vector space is an inner product, i.e. a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form'. Counterexample: let (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an eta-orthonormal basis, whose existence is the orthonormal-basis lemma. The vector e_0 is nonzero but eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 < 0, so eta is not positive definite and hence is not an inner product; consequently eta does not induce a norm, and the positive-definite inner-product theory (Cauchy-Schwarz, norms, orthogonal projection) cannot be applied to eta without additional argument.
items.strategy: A single evaluation refutes positive definiteness: e_0 is nonzero and eta(e_0,e_0) = -1 by the definition of an eta-orthonormal basis. The definition of an inner product requires positive-definiteness, so the refutation is immediate.

items.title: Worked construction of a future-oriented inertial frame from an arbitrary orthonormal basis
items.statement: Worked example of the sign and orientation adjustments. In an eta-orthonormal ordered basis (f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3) with f_0 timelike but past (f_0 in C^-) and with the ordered basis negatively oriented, the frame (o; -f_0, f_1, f_2, f_3) has first vector future and flips the orientation class, so it is positively oriented -- and if the original orientation was already positive, one replaces f_1 by -f_1 instead (or swaps f_1, f_2), which preserves eta-orthonormality and the future first vector and flips the orientation. Explicit 1+1-dimensional case: with eta = diag(-1,1), f_0 = (-1,0) (past timelike), f_1 = (0,1) (spacelike); then (-f_0, f_1) = ((1,0),(0,1)) satisfies eta(-f_0,-f_0) = -1, eta(f_1,f_1) = +1, eta(-f_0,f_1) = 0, and -f_0 is future, so it is an inertial frame of the model.
items.strategy: Use the defining properties: negating a vector preserves eta-orthonormality and changes the change-of-basis determinant by the factor -1; the timelike set is the disjoint union of C^+ and C^-, so exactly one of f_0, -f_0 is future. The 1+1 example is checked by direct evaluation of the displayed diagonal form.

items.title: Complex plane-wave fields: real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Fix $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, $\omega>0$ and $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Writing $\exp$ for the complex exponential, $\operatorname{Re}$ for the real part and $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$ for the Euclidean inner product, define for each $t\in\mathbb R$ the real vector fields $$\mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf e\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr],\qquad \mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf b\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr]$$ on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise. Complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations; the complex object is not itself a physical field, and real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are explicit operations.
items.strategy: State the encoding convention and its regularity: the defining maps are smooth in $(\mathbf x,t)$ because the complex exponential is entire and $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t$ is linear. No electromagnetic interpretation is asserted; that is a later model choice.

J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Moving parametrized surface patches and their flux
items.statement: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary orientation and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval. Let $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extend to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior, and require the images to be embedded if an actual material sheet is intended. Define the velocity $v$ on a neighbourhood of the swept surface by $v(r(u,v,t),t):=\partial_tr(u,v,t)$, requiring it to be single-valued and of class $C^1$. For a $C^1$ field $B$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the flux through the patch at time $t$ is $$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,v,t),t),\,r_u(u,v,t)\times r_v(u,v,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv.$$
items.strategy: Elementary Green regions are compact Jordan-measurable parameter regions, so the flux is a Riemann integral, and the orientation is the patch orientation of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. Single-valuedness of the velocity is the hypothesis that makes the transport formula of the moving-flux lemma well posed. No physical assertion is made.

J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)

items.title: Surface distributions and interfacial jumps
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$, and put $\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the surface integral being that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. A continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$. Both functionals are continuous of finite order on test functions, because $\lvert a\rvert$ and $\psi$ are bounded on the compact interface and the surface measure is finite. A field that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided continuous traces has locally integrable components; write $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ for the jump across $S$.
items.strategy: Use the compact surface integral definition and the finite-order estimate for continuous densities; for non-compact interfaces localize with a compactly supported test. The jump $[F]$ is the one-sided trace difference, and the sign convention of $n$ (minus to plus) is fixed here and used by the interface-derivative lemma.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Localization: vanishing integrals or fluxes force a continuous function to vanish
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous. If $\int_Vg=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Moreover, if $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous and the flux of $F$ through every planar disk in each of the three coordinate planes, of every radius for which the closed disk lies in $U$, is zero, then $F=0$ on $U$.
items.strategy: If $g(p)_i>0$, continuity gives a ball $V\Subset U$ on which $g_i\ge g_i(p)/2$; then $0<(g_i(p)/2)\lambda(V)\le\int_Vg_i$, contradicting the hypothesis. Apply to each component and to $-g_i$. The disk statement applies the planar case to each coordinate component with the coordinate normal. One special loop or box does not suffice.

J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Monopole-dipole expansion with an explicit remainder for compactly supported $L^1$ densities
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ vanish outside $\{y:\lvert y\rvert\le a\}$. Put $Q:=\int\rho$, $p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,dy$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert$. Then for every $x$ with $r:=\lvert x\rvert\ge2a>0$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{\lvert x-y\rvert}\,dy=\frac Qr+\frac{p\cdot x}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad \lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$
items.strategy: Set $h(s)=\lvert x-sy\rvert^{-1}$; $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ and the identity $h(1)-h(0)-h'(0)=\int_0^1(1-s)h''(s)\,ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem applied to $\frac{d}{ds}[(1-s)h'(s)+h(s)]=(1-s)h''(s)$. Because $\lvert x-sy\rvert\ge r-a\ge r/2$ for $r\ge2a$, one has $\lvert h''(s)\rvert\le4\lvert y\rvert^2/(r-a)^3\le32\lvert y\rvert^2/r^3$, and integrating against $\lvert\rho\rvert$ gives the bound with $C=16$, which is permissible but not sharp. The published far-field theorem supplies the leading $Q/r$ term only.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
S. Teitel, PHY 415 (University of Rochester), Unit 2-4: Electric Multipole Expansion

items.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
items.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, let $a<b$, and let $f$ and $\partial_tf$ be continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, with relative derivatives at the endpoints, and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$. The same conclusion holds, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], with surface measure on a fixed compact $C^1$ hypersurface in place of $K$ and Lebesgue measure. Nothing is asserted for moving parameter sets or for singularities crossing $K$.
items.strategy: For fixed $x$ the mean value theorem writes $[f(x,t+h)-f(x,t)]/h=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$ for some $\tau$ between $t$ and $t+h$; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact product bounds the integral of the difference by the sup-error times the finite measure. Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
items.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^1$ with graph contained in an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$. For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $$\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_Iz'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,$$ the integrands having compact support in $I$. Then $\rho,J\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$.
items.strategy: Pair the divergence with a test: $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]\,dt=-q\int_I\frac{d}{dt}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt=0$, since $t\mapsto\psi(z(t),t)$ is $C^1$ with compact support. The chain rule supplies the derivative. Only prescribed point support is proved; Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted.

items.title: Quadratic stress identity and the local angular-balance identity
items.statement: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$. Put $Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $(\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_j\partial_jQ_{ij}$. Then $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$. Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($+1$ on even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ on odd ones, $0$ otherwise), every $C^1$ symmetric tensor satisfies $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0$, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ with $\Pi$ symmetric, $\operatorname{div}\Pi$ taken as $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_\ell\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$, then $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$.
items.strategy: Expand $\sum_j\partial_j(F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2)=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_jF_j\partial_jF_i-\sum_jF_j\partial_iF_j$ by the product rule; the last difference is $-(F\times\operatorname{curl}F)_i$. For the second part, expand $\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}$ and cancel the two equal terms using symmetry; the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes. No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is needed.

items.title: Distributional divergence and curl across a stationary interface
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $S\subset\Omega$ be a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, and let $F$ be $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces on $S$. Then, away from the edge $\partial S$ and in the distributional sense, $$\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S,\qquad \operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\,\delta_S,$$ where the bracket terms denote the locally integrable functions equal to the classical divergence and curl on each open side and $[F]=F_+-F_-$.
items.strategy: Against a test supported away from the edge, split $-\int F\cdot\nabla\psi$ into the two sides and apply the divergence theorem to $\psi F$ on each side; the outward normal is $n$ on the minus side and $-n$ on the plus side, so the boundary terms combine to $(F_+-F_-)\cdot n$. Componentwise integration by parts gives $\partial_iF_j=\{\partial_iF_j\}+n_i[F_j]\delta_S$, and antisymmetrizing the index pair gives the curl formula. A moving interface needs a separate account.

S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3

items.title: Joint regularity of radial vector and scalar potentials on star-shaped domains
items.statement: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$. Then the radial witness $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$, then the radial scalar witness $\phi(x,t):=\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. For $C^\infty$ data both potentials are $C^\infty$ jointly. No global potential on an arbitrary open set is claimed.
items.strategy: Repeat the compact-rectangle parameter-differentiation argument for every derivative through order $k$; the parameter derivatives are continuous on the compact rectangle $[0,1]\times$-slices, so the radial witness is $C^k$ jointly. The scalar clause applies the published Poincaré lemma and its radial witness. On a ball the construction is local even when $U$ has holes; first and second cohomological obstructions must not be conflated.

references.title: J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Transport of flux through a moving patch
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]], let $B$ be a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of the swept surface with $\operatorname{div}B=0$. Then $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$ and $$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$ the boundary integral using the induced orientation. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term $\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$ appears.
items.strategy: Differentiate the parametrized flux with the parameter lemma; the area derivative contributes $\partial_uv\times r_v+r_u\times\partial_vv$, and collecting terms gives $[\partial_tB+(v\cdot\nabla)B+B\operatorname{div}v-(B\cdot\nabla)v]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$. The published cross-product identity turns this into $[\partial_tB+v\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$, and patch Stokes converts the curl term into the boundary circulation. The $C^2$ hypothesis lets mixed derivatives commute. Lorentz-force interpretation is a separate physical premise.

items.title: Period averages of products of real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Let $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, and let $a,d\in\mathbb C$ (or $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, componentwise). Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d),$$ and the dot-product and cross-product versions hold componentwise. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation.
items.strategy: Write $\operatorname{Re}(z)=(z+\overline z)/2$; the product is one constant term $\frac14(a\overline d+\overline ad)$ plus oscillatory terms $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$, which integrate to zero over a full period by the fundamental theorem applied to $e^{\pm2i\omega t}/(\pm2i\omega)$.

items.title: The two-equation interface system at normal incidence
items.statement: Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for $j=1,2$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$ Then $E_r/E_i=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$, $E_t/E_i=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, and $R:=\lvert E_r/E_i\rvert^2$, $T:=(Z_1/Z_2)\lvert E_t/E_i\rvert^2$ satisfy $R+T=1$. The two equations are assumed, not derived; oblique incidence, complex impedance and anisotropy require further systems and branch conventions.
items.strategy: Solve the $2\times2$ system by substitution; its determinant is $Z_1+Z_2>0$. For $R+T=1$, substitute the ratios and use $(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2=(Z_1+Z_2)^2$. No electromagnetic validity is asserted.

references.title: R. Fitzpatrick, Electromagnetism lecture notes (UT Austin), Reflection at a dielectric boundary, Eqs. (1210)-(1232)

items.title: Explicit mathematical hypothesis and convention examples for the elementary prerequisites
items.statement: Take $D=[0,1]^2$, $a\in C^2(I)$ with $a>0$, $r(u,v,t)=(a(t)u,a(t)v,0)$, $B=e_3$ and $v=(a'/a)(x_1,x_2,0)$. The parametrized flux is $a^2$, so its derivative is $2aa'$. The fixed-time surface integral of $B_t$ is $0$, while $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=-2(a'/a)e_3$; patch Stokes therefore gives $\oint(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf l=-2aa'$, exactly the sign in the moving-flux lemma. Treating this moving patch as fixed would falsely give zero. All fields and maps are smooth at the stated regularity, and no singular support is involved.
items.strategy: Verify each display by direct computation at the stated regularity. The example checks the sign convention of the moving-flux lemma and the necessity of the motion term; it does not assert any physical law.

items.title: The Minkowski affine four-space: the form $\eta$, causal cones, frames and Lorentz maps
items.statement: With $\mathbb R^4$ the space of functions $4\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-function-space]]) put $V:=\mathbb R^4$, and let $A$ be the set $\mathbb R^4$ together with the map $V\times A\to A$, $(v,p)\mapsto v+p$, given by function addition; then $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$, $0+p=p$, and for all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$ ([[def-vector-space]]), so $A$ is an affine space with translation space $V$. Fix the ordered basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ with $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and $0$ otherwise, and write $v=v_0e_0+\dots+v_3e_3$ ([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). The **Minkowski form** is $\eta(v,w):=-v_0w_0+v_1w_1+v_2w_2+v_3w_3$; it is the standard bilinear form of [[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first coordinate reversed and the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates, so it is a symmetric bilinear form ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]) whose matrix in $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; that matrix is invertible, so $\eta$ is nondegenerate ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]). A vector $v\ne0$ is **timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$ and **spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and then $v_0\ne0$, so it is **future-directed** when $v_0>0$ and **past-directed** when $v_0<0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Put $C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v_0>0\}$ for the **future causal cone**. The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ ([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]). A **Lorentz map** is an invertible linear $L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) with $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; in the basis above this is exactly $L^{\mathsf T}\eta L=\eta$, where $\eta$ also denotes $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the transpose is [[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]], by [[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] (a linear map preserving $\eta$ is automatically invertible because $\eta$ is nondegenerate). $L$ is **proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and **orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$; a **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ with an ordered basis $(u_0,\dots,u_3)$ of $V$ satisfying $\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ and $u_0\in C^+$, and the **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique $(x^0,\dots,x^3)$ with $p=o+x^0u_0+\dots+x^3u_3$. A **tensor of type $(p,q)$** on $V$ is a multilinear map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$, not an array: vectors are the $(1,0)$ case, covectors the $(0,1)$ case and two-forms the skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ case, and under the coordinate change $x'=Lx$ of the frame by a Lorentz map $L$ the components satisfy $v'=Lv$, $\theta'=(L^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\theta$ and $F'(v,w)=F(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w)$. Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate $x^0$ has the dimension of length and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$.
items.strategy: Direct definition with the elementary verifications recorded where they belong to the definition: bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$ from its coordinate formula, nondegeneracy from the invertible matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the implication $\eta(v,v)\le0$ and $v\ne0$ $\Rightarrow$ $v_0\ne0$ from $v_0^2\ge v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2$, and the matrix form $\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\iff L^{\mathsf T}\eta L=\eta$ from the congruence law for the matrix of a bilinear form under a change of basis. No physical claim is made; identifying $A$ with physical spacetime and $c$ with the speed of light in vacuum is a later physical premise.

items.title: The explicit Lorentz boost preserves $\eta$, has determinant $1$ and preserves the future cone
items.statement: Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define $\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_1=\gamma(v_1-\beta v_0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_2=v_2$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)_3=v_3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$; (d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$ for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.
items.strategy: Substitution in the coordinate formula of $\eta$ gives $-\gamma^2(v_0-\beta v_1)^2+\gamma^2(v_1-\beta v_0)^2=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)(-v_0^2+v_1^2)$ with the last two coordinates unchanged, and $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$; the $0$–$1$ block of the matrix has determinant $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ and the remaining block is the identity, giving $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; for future causal $v$ one has $|v_1|\le\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2}\le v_0$ from $\eta(v,v)\le0$, and $0\le\beta<1$ gives $(\Lambda_\beta v)_0=\gamma(v_0-\beta v_1)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v_0>0$, so $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; applying the same argument to $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ and using $\Lambda_\beta\Lambda_{-\beta}=\mathrm{id}$ (again $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$) gives equality. No empirical relativity principle is proved.

Sean M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity (arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1), Chapter 1, printed pp. 1–30

items.title: Proper time along a $C^1$ future timelike curve: strictly increasing reparametrization with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$
items.statement: Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and $z^0{}'(s)>0$ for every $s\in J$; $z'$ is the derivative of the vector-valued curve ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) and such a $z$ is called a $C^1$ future timelike curve. Put $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, fix $s_0\in J$, and define $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$ for $s\in J$. Then: (1) $g$ is continuous on $J$ and so is $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$, where $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); (2) $\tau$ is differentiable on $J$ with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$, hence $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $J$, injective, and continuous ([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]], [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]); (3) the inverse $\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of the interval $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$ ([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]); (4) the reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s)):=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ satisfying $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]); (5) if instead $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$ and $\tau$ is not injective, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization ([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]); (6) if $z(s)=p+sv$ with $\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v_0>0$, then $\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)$ and $U=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]]). The identification of such straight lines with inertial motion is a physical premise and is not asserted here.
items.strategy: $C^1$ gives continuity of the components $z^a{}'$ and [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] passes between the vector-valued and component statements; the four squares $(z^a{}')^2$ and their signed sum are continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $g$ is continuous; $\sqrt g$ is continuous because squaring is a continuous injection of $[0,\infty)$ onto itself with continuous inverse $\sqrt{\cdot}$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]], [[thm-continuous-inverse]]), and composition preserves continuity. [[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]] makes $\tau$ a primitive of the continuous function $c^{-1}\sqrt g$ on $J$, giving (2) with [[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]; [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] (hypotheses: $\tau$ continuous and injective on the interval $J$, $\tau'(s)\ne0$) gives (3); [[thm-chain-rule]] applied to the components of $z\circ\tau^{-1}$ and reassembled gives (4), where $\eta(U,U)=(c^2/g)\eta(z',z')=-c^2$ uses bilinearity and symmetry of $\eta$; (5) is the zero integrand case; (6) is direct computation with constant $z'=v$.

items.title: Antisymmetric contractions vanish and $mU'=q\Phi(U)$ preserves $\eta(U,U)$
items.statement:
Let $F:V	imes V	o\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form, $F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with $\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(u,w)$ for all $w\in V$ ([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]], [[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and $\Phi:V	o V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); in a frame $\Phi(u)^\mu=\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha eta}u^ eta$, the index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_
u u^
u=0$. Consequently, if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J	o V$ is differentiable ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on $J$ for some real $m
e0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). This is a conditional statement about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any particle.
items.strategy: $\eta(\Phi(u),u)=F(u,u)=0$ by skew-symmetry, and $\eta$ is symmetric, so $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$. For the second claim $f(s):=\eta(U(s),U(s))=\sum_a\epsilon_a(U^a(s))^2$ with $\epsilon=(-1,1,1,1)$ is differentiable on the open interval $J$ with $f'=2\sum_a\epsilon_aU^a(U^a)'=2\eta(U,U')$ by the product rule, and $\eta(U,U')=(q/m)\eta(U,\Phi(U))=0$; a differentiable function on an interval with vanishing derivative is constant.

items.statement: With $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$: (i) $v=(1,0,0,0)$ is future timelike and unit, $\eta(v,v)=-1$. (ii) For $0<\beta<1$ the boost $\Lambda_\beta$ of [[lem-em-boost-preserves-metric]] sends $v$ to $(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$, whose $\eta$-norm is $-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$ and whose time component $\gamma$ is positive; at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined, so the hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped. (iii) The null line $z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, has $\eta(z',z')=0$, so the proper-time construction of [[lem-em-proper-time-reparametrization]] gives $\tau\equiv0$, which is not an invertible parameter: the timelike hypothesis cannot be weakened to causal. No physical clock premise or experimental claim is used.
items.strategy: Four direct computations in the fixed standard frame: evaluation of $\eta$ on the given vectors, substitution of $v$ in the boost formula, the vanishing of the null tangent, and the identification $\Phi=\mathrm{id}$ when $F=\eta$ (uniqueness in the defining property of $\Phi$). items.title: The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations for continuous coefficients
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. If $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R^m)$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Here $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product and $\int_U\langle g,h\rangle\,d\lambda$ is the finite sum $\sum_{i<m}\int_U g_ih_i\,d\lambda$ of integrals of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). The scalar case is $m=1$: a continuous $g$ with $\int_Ugh\,d\lambda=0$ for every $h\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$ vanishes on $U$. The vector case is deduced from the scalar case componentwise, each component tested separately. The conclusion is pointwise on $U$, and the hypothesis is the full family of compactly supported smooth test functions. The Axiom of Countable Choice is declared because the localization lemma [[lem-em-continuous-localization]] and the measurability fact [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]] used in the recorded proof assume it; no other choice principle enters.
items.strategy:
Scalar case. Suppose $g(p)
e0$ for some $p\in U$; replacing $g$ by $-g$, which satisfies the same hypothesis, assume $g(p)>0$. Openness of $U$ and continuity of $g$ at $p$ give $r>0$ with $B(p,r)\subseteq U$ and $g\ge g(p)/2$ on $B(p,r)$. Apply the cutoff lemma to the compact set $\{p\}$ inside the open ball $B(p,r)$: it yields $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B(p,r))$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighbourhood of $p$, so $\chi(p)=1$ and $\chi$ extends by zero to a test function in $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $\varphi:=g\chi$ is continuous on $U$ as a product of continuous real functions, satisfies $\varphi\ge0$ because $g>0$ on the support of $\chi$, and has $\varphi(p)=g(p)>0$, so $\varphi
e0$. Were $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$: the localization lemma applied to the continuous function $\varphi$ (contrapositive form of [[lem-em-continuous-localization]]) produces a ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$ with $\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda
e0$; since $\varphi\ge0$ this integral is positive, and monotonicity of the nonnegative integral gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda\ge\int_V\varphi\,d\lambda>0$, contradicting $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=0$. But $\chi$ is an admissible test function, so the hypothesis gives $\int_U\varphi\,d\lambda=\int_U g\chi\,d\lambda=0$; hence no point $p$ with $g(p)
e0$ exists. Vector case. For each $i<m$ and each $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U;\mathbb R)$, apply the hypothesis to $h=\psi e_i$ to get $\int_U g_i\psi\,d\lambda=0$; the scalar case gives $g_i=0$. Measurability of $\varphi$ comes from continuity, and the positive-integral comparison uses the order rules for the nonnegative integral. Continuity is retained verbatim: a measurable $g$ that is $0$ almost everywhere but not everywhere passes every test pairing without being the zero function, so the pointwise conclusion genuinely uses continuity.

items.title: Hypothesis and convention boundaries for the variational prerequisites
items.statement:
Two exact boundary checks. (i) Stationarity is first order. On $\mathbb R^2$ the polynomial $S(x,y)=x^2-y^2$ has differential $0$ at $(0,0)$, while $S(\varepsilon,0)=\varepsilon^2>0$ and $S(0,\varepsilon)=-\varepsilon^2<0$ for every $\varepsilon
e0$; a point where the first variation vanishes need not be a minimum. Consequently the equivalence of [[lem-em-compact-field-variation]] between stationarity and the coefficient equation, and the conversion by [[lem-em-fundamental-variation-lemma]] of a vanishing first variation into pointwise equations, are first-order conditions: they carry no minimality and no existence content, and the example involves no adopted physical action. (ii) Compact support of the variation is essential. Take $U=(-1,1)^4$, $\kappa=1$, $J=0$ and the smooth field $A$ with $A_0(x)=(x^1)^2$ and $A_1=A_2=A_3=0$, in the conventions of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]]. Then $F_{01}=-2x^1$ and $F^{01}=\eta^{00}\eta^{11}F_{01}=2x^1$, all other components vanishing, so $\partial_\mu F^{\mu0}=\partial_1F^{10}=-2
e0$ and the coefficient equation $\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=-\kappa J^
u$ fails at $
u=0$. Nevertheless the variation $h$ with $h_0\equiv1$ and $h_1=h_2=h_3=0$ is smooth but not compactly supported in $U$; along it $A_0+sh_0=(x^1)^2+s$, so $F_{01}$ and the integrand $L=2(x^1)^2$ are independent of $s$ and $S[A+sh]=\int_U2(x^1)^2\,d\lambda$ is constant in $s$, with first variation $0$ although the field equation fails. Hence the integration-by-parts conversion (b) and the stationarity equivalence (c) of the compact-field lemma hold for compactly supported variations only, and the compact-support hypothesis cannot be dropped.

items.title: Linear and affine Lorentz maps, and the Lorentz group
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (d) An affine Lorentz map is a map F: A -> A for which there exist p_0 in A and a linear Lorentz map L with F(p_0 + v) = F(p_0) + L v for all v in V; equivalently F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) for all p in A, and L is then unique. F is called proper (resp. orthochronous) when L is. If x is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x(F(p)) = M x(p) + b for all p, where M is the matrix of L in the frame's ordered basis and b := x(F(o)) - M x(o) in R^4. (e) In this framework, unless stated otherwise, 'Lorentz transformation' means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map; improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly (the B-page counterexample names the parity and time-reversal matrices).
items.strategy: A definition item: it fixes the language of the page and makes no proof claim beyond what lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure establishes (the matrix criterion, invertibility and the group structure, which is listed as justified_by). The well-definedness obligations are: (i) the set O(V,eta) is defined by a property of linear maps on the fixed vector space V, so it is a set; (ii) the matrix criterion in (b) must be stated in an ordered eta-orthonormal basis, whose existence is the cited lemma, and its independence of that choice is part of the proved content; (iii) 'L(C^+) = C^+' is a condition on a map of sets, not a notation for an unproved continuity statement; (iv) the affine definition (d) must distinguish an active map F on the point set A from the coordinate expression in a chart, and must not conflate an affine map with a general chart change; the coordinate expression requires the identification of vectors with coordinate columns and the cited matrix conventions. The exposition may state that the linear part of an affine Lorentz map is recovered as L v = F(p+v) - F(p), independently of p.

items.title: The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta
items.statement: Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), and let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be its coordinates, so that a vector is written x = x^0 e_0 + x^1 e_1 + x^2 e_2 + x^3 e_3 and the spatial part is the coordinate column x_vec = (x^1,x^2,x^3) of R^3 with its standard Euclidean structure (def-euclidean-inner-product). For beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1, where |beta| is the Euclidean norm, set gamma(beta) := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) > 1 (def-rational-power, lem-rational-power-laws). The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta is the linear map B(beta): V -> V defined by its action on coordinates: for beta not equal to 0, x'^0 = gamma (x^0 - beta . x),  x' = x + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . x) beta - gamma beta x^0, and for beta = 0, B(0) := identity, where x' denotes the coordinates of B(beta) applied to the vector with coordinates x, and beta . x is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) the matrix of B(beta) is B^0_0 = gamma, B^0_i = B^i_0 = -gamma beta_i for i = 1,2,3, and B^i_j = delta^i_j + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) beta_i beta_j for i,j = 1,2,3 (with the last expression replaced by delta^i_j for beta = 0; its beta -> 0 limit is (1/2) beta_i beta_j). In the 1+1 case beta = beta e_1 this reads x'^0 = gamma(x^0 - beta x^1), x'^1 = gamma(x^1 - beta x^0). The vector beta is called the boost parameter; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention.
items.strategy: A definition item, well-defined because the displayed formulas assign to every coordinate pair (x^0,x_vec) a pair (x'^0,x'_vec), and by thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis (applied through def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map) there is a unique linear map with that matrix, namely x |-> E o M o E^{-1}. The beta = 0 case is declared separately because the matrix expression ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) is undefined there; the definition must not silently divide by zero, and the extension is not asserted to be continuous (that is a separate computation). This item asserts no Lorentz property: that B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and that B(-beta) is its inverse is the content of lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse, and the composition law is the content of lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition; the physical reading of c beta as a relative velocity is stated only on the physics items of this page, not here.
